subject: physics
question_text: Obtain an expression for the work done during an adiabatic process. A quantity of heat 6 × 10⁵ J is supplied to a system at constant pressure 10⁵ N/m². If the volume of the system increases from 3 m³ to 5 m³, calculate the work done by the system and the change in its internal energy.

mark_split.label: What this means for internal energy

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Long Answer Question 2 (printed p.132). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The eight 1-mark step split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: the adiabatic relation PV^γ = constant, the integral W = ∫P dV reaching W = (P₁V₁ − P₂V₂)/(γ−1) = nR(T₁−T₂)/(γ−1), the first-law consequence W = −ΔU for ΔQ = 0, and the constant-pressure numerical W = PΔV = 10⁵ × 2 = 2 × 10⁵ J with ΔU = Q − W = 6×10⁵ − 2×10⁵ = 4×10⁵ J all match the standard NCERT Class-11 Chapter 12 (Thermodynamics) treatment.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The adiabatic condition
lines: In an adiabatic process no heat
where γ = C_P/C_V for the gas.
steps.margin_note: First mark. State ΔQ = 0 and write PV^γ = constant.
steps.why: This is the one relation that replaces PV = constant (isothermal) for a process with no heat exchange, and every later step is built on it.
common_mistakes: Writing PV = constant instead of PV^γ — that is the isothermal relation, not the adiabatic one.
Forgetting to state ΔQ = 0 — that is what makes the process adiabatic in the first place.

recall.must_convey: That an adiabatic process has ΔQ = 0, and that P and V are related by PV to the power gamma equals a constant.
accept: adiabatic means no heat exchange
delta Q equals zero
P V to the power gamma is constant
gamma is C_P by C_V

steps.memory_tip: Adiabatic means no heat: PVᵞ = constant, with the extra γ isothermal does not have.

steps.label: Set up the work integral
lines: The work done by the gas as it
expands from V₁ to V₂ is
From PV^γ = k, write P in terms
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Write W as ∫P dV, and P as k/V^γ.
steps.why: Work is always the area under a P-V curve, so writing P purely as a function of V is what lets the adiabatic curve itself be integrated.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate with both P and V as independent variables — P must be written as a function of V first.
Losing the constant k — it carries the values P₁V₁^γ (equally P₂V₂^γ) needed later.

recall.must_convey: That the work is the integral of P dV from V one to V two, with P written as k over V to the gamma using the adiabatic constant.
accept: work is the integral of P dV
P equals k over V to the gamma
integrate from V one to V two
area under the P V curve
reject: P V to the power gamma is constant

steps.memory_tip: Work is the area under the curve, so write P in terms of V first.

steps.label: Integrate
lines: V₁ to V₂ and substituting back
k = P₁V₁^γ = P₂V₂^γ at the two
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Integrate, substitute the limits, box the result.
steps.why: Substituting P₁V₁^γ and P₂V₂^γ back for k at the two limits is what turns the integral into a formula written purely in the measurable quantities P₁, V₁, P₂ and V₂.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer in terms of k instead of substituting P₁V₁^γ and P₂V₂^γ back in.
Dropping the sign, writing W = (P₂V₂ − P₁V₁)/(γ − 1) — for an expansion this must come out positive.

recall.must_convey: That integrating and substituting the limits gives W equal to P one V one minus P two V two, divided by gamma minus one.
accept: integrate P equals k V to minus gamma
W is P one V one minus P two V two over gamma minus one
substitute the limits V one and V two
the boxed work formula
reject: work equals nR times T one minus T two
heard_as: P one V one minus P two V two

steps.memory_tip: The boxed form has P₁V₁ first, then P₂V₂, over γ − 1.

steps.label: Rewrite using the gas equation
lines: For n moles, PV = nRT at each end
of the process, so P₁V₁ = nRT₁
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Substitute PV = nRT at both limits.
steps.why: The pressure-volume form and the temperature form are the same result — writing it in T₁ and T₂ is the version wanted when temperatures, rather than pressures and volumes, are given.
common_mistakes: Substituting PV = nRT only at one end of the process, not both.
Writing T₂ − T₁ instead of T₁ − T₂ — for an expansion the gas cools, so T₁ is the larger temperature.

recall.must_convey: That substituting PV = nRT at both limits rewrites the work as nR times T one minus T two, over gamma minus one.
accept: P V equals n R T at both ends
W is nR T one minus T two over gamma minus one
rewrite in terms of temperature
P one V one is nRT one
reject: W is P one V one minus P two V two over gamma minus one
heard_as: nR T one minus T two

steps.memory_tip: Same result, two forms: swap P₁V₁ and P₂V₂ for nRT₁ and nRT₂.

steps.label: What this means for internal energy
lines: In an adiabatic expansion the gas
does positive work, so ΔU is
out of the internal energy, and
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Apply the first law with ΔQ = 0 and state the gas cools.
steps.why: This is the physical meaning of the formula just derived: with no heat supplied, the ONLY source of the work done is the gas's own internal energy, so its temperature must fall as it expands.
common_mistakes: Saying the temperature stays the same in an adiabatic expansion — that is the isothermal case; here the gas cools.
Missing the sign: work done BY the gas is positive, so ΔU = −W is negative, a decrease.

recall.must_convey: That with ΔQ = 0 the first law gives W equals minus ΔU, so the work in an adiabatic expansion comes out of the internal energy and the gas cools.
accept: delta Q is zero so W equals minus delta U
the work comes out of the internal energy
the gas cools in an adiabatic expansion
first law with no heat exchange
reject: W is nR T one minus T two over gamma minus one

steps.memory_tip: No heat in, so the work has nowhere else to come from but ΔU.

steps.label: Work at constant pressure
lines: A system is held at constant
work done by the system is
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. W = PΔV with ΔV = 2 m³, giving 2 × 10⁵ J.
steps.why: This is a separate, constant-pressure process — the work is the simple W = PΔV of an isobaric change, not the adiabatic formula above, because here pressure, not heat, is held fixed.
common_mistakes: Reaching for the adiabatic work formula from part one — this process is at constant pressure, so W = PΔV applies directly.
Using ΔV = 5 m³ instead of the change 5 − 3 = 2 m³.

recall.must_convey: That at constant pressure 10 to the five, with volume changing by 2 cubic metres, the work done is 2 times 10 to the five joules.
accept: work is P delta V
10 to the five times two
the work is 2 times 10 to the five joules
constant pressure work
reject: W equals nR T one minus T two over gamma minus one

steps.memory_tip: Constant pressure: work is just P times the change in volume.

steps.label: Apply the first law
lines: ΔQ = ΔU + W rearranges to give
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Rearrange the first law to ΔU = Q − W.
steps.why: The heat supplied splits between raising the internal energy and doing external work — rearranging the first law isolates the internal-energy change the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Writing ΔU = Q + W — the work done BY the system is subtracted, not added.
Using the adiabatic work formula's W here instead of the 2 × 10⁵ J just found for this constant-pressure process.

recall.must_convey: That the first law rearranges to delta U equals Q minus W.
accept: delta U equals Q minus W
rearrange the first law
heat in minus work done
delta Q equals delta U plus W rearranged
heard_as: delta U equals Q minus W

steps.memory_tip: Heat in splits two ways: rearrange ΔQ = ΔU + W to ΔU = Q − W.

steps.label: The change in internal energy
steps.margin_note: Eighth mark. Substitute and box ΔU = 4 × 10⁵ J.
steps.why: This is the number the question asks for: of the 6 × 10⁵ J supplied, 2 × 10⁵ J left the system as work and the remaining 4 × 10⁵ J stayed behind as internal energy.
common_mistakes: Substituting the wrong work value — this is the 2 × 10⁵ J found for THIS constant-pressure process, not any adiabatic formula.
Losing a power of ten when subtracting 2 × 10⁵ from 6 × 10⁵.

recall.must_convey: That substituting gives ΔU equal to 6 times 10 to the five minus 2 times 10 to the five, which is 4 times 10 to the five joules.
accept: 6 times 10 to the five minus 2 times 10 to the five
delta U is 4 times 10 to the five joules
the internal energy increases by 4 times 10 to the five
final answer 4 times 10 to the five joules
reject: work is 2 times 10 to the five joules

steps.memory_tip: 6 in, 2 out as work, 4 stays behind as internal energy — all ×10⁵ J.

insider_note: The numerical is a separate constant-pressure process, not adiabatic — use W = PΔV directly rather than reaching for the formula from the derivation.
